newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finns say EU may wither as EMU lacks legitimacy.
newsitem.headline: Finns say EU may wither as EMU lacks legitimacy.

text.p: The European Union could disintegrate due to pressures caused by legitimacy problems linked to economic and monetary union and the planned European central bank, a study by a Finnish think-tank said on Wednesday.

"From the legitimacy point of view, the European single market project, to be completed with the single currency and central bank, is an inherently contradictory one," senior researcher Heikki Patomaki at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs wrote in a new book called "The Politics of Economic and Monetary Union".
The third phase of EMU amounted to a transfer of authority from national bodies to central European bodies justified by "the alleged benefits of the single market," he said.

"One should perhaps expect these reforms to deepen the legitimation problems of the EU. In the longer run, one possible outcome of this might be the -- partial? -- disintegration of the Union," he added.

In the public eye, "the convergence criteria, the aim of economic stability, and the priority given to the fight against inflation are widely perceived to be co-causing unemployment and social and fiscal dumping," Patomaki said.

Another reason for EMU opposition was the view of the single currency as a federalist project amid, he said, still 40 years after the EU's founding treaty of Rome, "a lack of solidarity and "we" feeling in the Union."

Pro-EMU politicians' "quest for a justification that is now lacking might lead ... to an actual and more widespread legitimation crisis of EMU and even of the European Union as a political rule," Patomaki said.
Through its move towards an independent and unaccountable central bank the EU was undermining the conditions for finding new sources of legitimation for itself, he said.

In another of the book's seven articles, Teivo Teivainen, lecturer at the Helsinki University, wrote that in the field of monetary policy, Europe's democratic institutions would be left with "basically decorative functions".
The creation of a European Central Bank would transfer governance to "unelected and non-accountable bodies," he said.
And Stephen Gill, political sciences professor at York University in Toronto, Canada, wrote that EMU "eats away at processes of political accountability and democracy."
The obsession with zero inflation reflected the interests of institutional investors, banks and multinational firms, he said.

The book said that the substance of the EU's Maastricht Treaty, which lay the groundwork for EMU, was built "to a large extent on the ideas" of the European Roundtable of Industrialists (ERT) -- an association of Europe's 40 biggest multinationals.
It said EMU supporters argued that halting the EMU process would lead to credibility problems in the capital markets.

"(Their) argument is that the process should be seen as irreversible once it has been started, and one should acknowledge that there are no means for national economic policies anyway," the book said.
